creative.body:
If your doctor put you on Ozempic and then told you to take Miralax for the constipation — read this before you buy another bottle.

Those two products are working on two completely different parts of your body. And the gap between them is about six feet of intestine.

I know because I spent three months and $214 figuring that out the hard way.

I've been on Wegovy since last May. Down 41 pounds. My jeans fit again. People at church started telling me how great I looked. Everything was working except one thing.

I stopped going to the bathroom.

Not slowed down. Stopped. Seven days. Nine days. Once, eleven.

My doctor said take Miralax. I took Miralax. Nothing. She said take it twice a day. I took it twice a day. Still nothing.

So I added Colace. Then magnesium citrate at bedtime. Then fiber gummies in the morning because my coworker said they worked for her. Then I switched to psyllium husk because someone in a Facebook group said gummies don't have enough fiber to matter.

By October I had five products on my bathroom counter and I hadn't gone in eight days.

I stood in the Walgreens laxative aisle on a Tuesday night trying to pick between Dulcolax and senna tea and I realized I had no idea why I was there. I'd already tried four things. None of them worked. I was just buying a fifth one because I didn't know what else to do.

That was the moment it stopped being frustrating and started being something else. I wasn't confused anymore. I was exhausted. I was spending money and swallowing pills and drinking powders and nothing was moving and nobody could tell me why.

My husband asked me one night if I'd eaten dinner and I said yes. I hadn't. I'd stopped eating full meals because the pressure in my stomach was unbearable by evening and I figured if I ate less, there'd be less to get stuck. I was on a weight loss medication and I was starving myself on top of it. Not to lose weight. To avoid the pain of food sitting inside me for days.

I had a follow-up with my GI nurse practitioner in November. Routine visit. She asked how the Wegovy was going and I told her fine, except for the constipation. I listed everything I was taking. Miralax. Colace. Magnesium. Fiber. She let me finish.

Then she said something I hadn't heard from anyone.

"All of those work on your colon. Your problem isn't in your colon."

That was it. She didn't explain the whole thing. She told me that GLP-1 medications slow down the stomach, and that the constipation I was experiencing was a stomach problem, not a colon problem. She said I could look into it if I wanted to understand why nothing was helping.

So I did.

That night I sat at my kitchen table with my laptop and I searched "why do GLP-1 medications cause constipation." Not how to fix it. Why it happens. For the first time I wasn't looking for a product. I was looking for an explanation.

GLP-1 medications work by slowing down gastric emptying. That's the whole mechanism behind the appetite suppression. Your stomach holds food longer so you feel full longer. That's the point.

But when your stomach slows down too much, food doesn't just sit there quietly. It sits there and ferments. Bacteria break it down. Gas builds up. Your stomach distends. And the food that's supposed to move into your intestines and eventually reach your colon... doesn't get there. Or it gets there so slowly that everything downstream backs up.

The constipation isn't happening in the colon. It's starting in the stomach.

And every single product I'd been taking — Miralax, Colace, Dulcolax, magnesium, fiber — works on the colon.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften stool. But there was barely any stool in my colon to soften. The food was still sitting in my stomach.

Dulcolax triggers contractions in the colon wall. But there was nothing in my colon to push. It was contracting around empty space. That's why it gave me cramps with zero results.

Fiber adds bulk. But adding bulk to a system where the stomach has already stopped moving forward just made the backup worse. The pressure got worse. The bloating got worse. And nothing came out anyway.

Magnesium citrate does the same thing as Miralax — pulls water into the lower intestine. Same organ. Same problem. Different brand name.

I'd spent three months taking four different products that all did the same thing to the same part of my body. A part of my body that wasn't even where the problem was.

Once I understood that, the question changed. It wasn't "which laxative should I try next." It was "what actually gets the stomach moving again."

And that's what I spent the next two hours reading about.

The first thing I found was a compound called apigenin. It's in celery juice extract. And what it does is help your stomach start moving again. Not the colon. The stomach. The actual part that GLP-1 medications are slowing down.

But that was only part of it. Because while food is sitting in the stomach fermenting, gas builds up. Sulfur compounds. That's the bloating, the distension, the feeling like you're inflated by dinner. So the second thing I found was chlorophyllin — it goes after those sulfur compounds and breaks them down. Deals with the gas that's been building up because the stomach isn't emptying.

And then the third piece. Once the stomach is moving again and the gas is handled, you need something to keep things flowing downstream. A prebiotic fiber — but not the kind that adds bulk to a backed-up system. The kind that feeds good bacteria in the lower gut so that when food finally does move through, the rest of the system is ready for it.

I went back to my bathroom and looked at every product on the counter. Miralax — nothing for the stomach. Colace — nothing for the stomach. The fiber I'd been choking down — nothing for the gas. Not one of those products did the first two things.

I found a small company called Motilli. Never heard of them. But they made a gummy specifically for people on GLP-1 medications. I almost didn't bother. I'd been burned too many times.

But I looked at the label. Celery juice extract — the apigenin source. Chlorophyllin. Prebiotic fiber. All three. In one gummy. Not a general probiotic. Not another colon product with new packaging. Something built around the actual cause.

I ordered one bottle.

The first four days, nothing. I figured I'd wasted my money again. Day five, I noticed the bloating was less intense by evening. I didn't think much of it.

Day nine, I went. On my own. No laxative. No magnesium the night before. I just woke up and went.

I sat there for a second afterward because I honestly couldn't remember the last time that had happened without me forcing it.

By the end of week three it was consistent. Not perfect. But consistent. Most mornings. No cramping. No emergency. No planning my day around whether my body would cooperate.

I ate a full dinner with my husband on a Friday night in December. Chicken, rice, vegetables. A normal plate. I didn't think about the pressure afterward. I didn't calculate whether I should skip breakfast the next day to compensate. I just ate and cleared my plate and we watched a movie and I forgot about my stomach entirely.

That hadn't happened in six months.

My sister started taking it in January. She's on Mounjaro. Same constipation. Same laxative graveyard. She called me after two weeks and said "I don't understand how this is different from everything else I've tried." I told her what the nurse practitioner told me. It's not working on your colon. It's working on your stomach. That's why it's different.

I walked past the laxative aisle at Walgreens last week. Didn't stop. Didn't even slow down. That aisle owned me for three months. Every Tuesday or Wednesday I'd be standing there reading boxes trying to figure out which one would be the one that finally worked.

They all worked. They all did exactly what they were supposed to do. They just did it to the wrong organ.

I'm a 54-year-old woman who spent $214 and three months on products that couldn't have helped me because they weren't designed for the problem I actually had.

If you're on a GLP-1 and you're rotating through laxatives and none of them are doing anything — it's not the products. It's not you. It's that the problem is in your stomach and everything you're taking works on your colon.

Motilli is the only thing I've found that works where the problem actually is. I wish someone had told me this in June instead of November. So I'm telling you now.
creative.title: I spent $214 on four different laxatives and they all did the same thing to the same organ
